summary: A command that puts one local file into a course. internal/client/upload.go is hand-authored and holds the whole three-request dance Canvas requires: POST /api/v1/courses/{id}/files asks where the file may go and comes back with an upload address, form fields to repeat and the name the file's own part must carry; a multipart POST to that address sends the bytes; and the redirect or Location that answers it is followed to get the file Canvas kept. internal/cli/upload.go is the command: upload <local-file> with --course, --folder, --name and --on-duplicate, printing {"action":"upload","course_id":...,"file":{...},"embed_src":"/courses/<id>/files/<id>/preview"}. root.go gains the AddCommand line, in the hand-authored block; the command carries a pp:path annotation of /api/v1/courses/{course_id}/files so Canvas Builder's untraceable-command hiding (sandbox-command-surface) keeps it visible by rule rather than by having no annotation. internal/client/formencode.go gains one clause at the top of railsBracketBody, extending form-encode-rails-bracket-params: a body of the new named type formBody is form-encoded whatever its key names look like. internal/gatewaytest/fake.go records each request's declared Content-Length, which is the only way a test can tell a streamed body with an exact length from a chunked one. The upload's own timeout is the client's plus a second per megabyte, so a large file is not cut off mid-stream by a bound set for a request whose body is a line of JSON.
reason: An agent writing a page needs somewhere to point an at, and a course file is the only such place inside Canvas Builder. Everything particular about this patch follows from the fact that the middle request of the three goes to an address Canvas names, not one this CLI composed. That address is checked before anything is built or dialed, and against a stricter rule than the client's general one: it must be allowed by the gateway and its path must be exactly /files_api, which is the only multipart body the gateway accepts from an agent (Plan D). A ticket pointing anywhere else is a ticket to hand the file, and the token carrying it, to something outside Canvas Builder, so that request returns a refusal and sends nothing. The redirect that answers the upload is checked the same way before it is followed. The upload is sent with CheckRedirect returning ErrUseLastResponse, because a redirect here is the answer rather than a hop: Canvas's local storage answers with a 302 to create_success, and following it automatically would re-send the whole file. A transport error on that request is an unknown outcome, never a retry — the bytes have already gone out, and the one thing worse than not knowing whether a file landed is landing it twice. The body is streamed. The upload_params come first in sorted key order, then the file's part, and the closing boundary is built by hand rather than taken from multipart.Writer.Close(), which would put it in front of the file. Content-Length is the exact sum of the three pieces, so a 50 MB upload costs 50 MB of disk reads and no memory. formBody exists because Canvas's file-create parameters are flat (name, size, content_type, on_duplicate) and railsBracketBody only form-encoded a body with a bracketed key, so these would have gone out as JSON and been at the mercy of Rails' parameter wrapping. The named type also means verifyWrite's map[string]any assertion does not match, which skips the post-write check on this one request — the right outcome, since step 1's answer is an upload ticket and carries none of the names sent, and it is noted in upload.go so it is not mistaken for an accident. In Canvas Builder the path argument must pass sandbox.Inside, which is what stops an agent uploading a file from outside the course folder, or a link inside it that points out, and --course defaults to the course that folder belongs to. Outside Canvas Builder --course is required rather than guessed.
known_limitations:
FileInfo reads a file's type from both "content-type" and "content_type", because Canvas spells it with a hyphen in the files API and with an underscore elsewhere; the hyphenated one wins when both are present. If Canvas ever sends both with different values for the same file, this picks the files API's spelling without saying so.

upload does not appear in `which` yet. whichIndex is generated and the curated capability index is Task 11's work, so for now the command is found through --help.

The large-file test holds about 100 MB briefly: gatewaytest.Fake reads each request body into memory before dispatching, and the assertion re-reads it to walk the multipart parts. Pointing upload_url at a second, streaming server would avoid that, but the gateway rule this patch exists to enforce forbids exactly that, so the test keeps the memory cost instead of weakening what it proves.

A 200 or 201 answer with no Location is read as the file itself, which is how S3-style storage behaves when it inlines the result. If some future Canvas answers the upload 200 with a body that is neither a file nor an error, the message says the upload was accepted without naming the file, which is accurate but gives the agent nothing to act on.

The folder is passed as parent_folder_path and never checked against the course's folders first, so a misspelled folder is whatever Canvas does with an unknown path (it creates it). Checking would cost a fourth request on every upload.
validated_outcome:
go build ./... and go vet ./... clean. go test ./... passing across every package on darwin/arm64 with Go 1.27.1. go test -race ./internal/client/ ./internal/cli/ ./internal/sandbox/ passing. golangci-lint run --max-issues-per-linter=0 --max-same-issues=0 reports nothing on internal/client/upload.go, internal/cli/upload.go, either test file or internal/gatewaytest/fake.go; the touched generated files report only their pre-existing findings. gofmt -l clean on every file in this patch.

One lint finding was real and was fixed rather than suppressed: bodyclose flagged the upload response, which sendUpload opened and uploadResult closed. The close now sits in the function that opened it, and uploadResult says so.

New coverage. internal/client/upload_test.go: TestUploadFileRefusesUploadURLOffGateway points upload_url at a second local server and asserts a RefusedError naming Canvas Builder's address, with that server seeing no connection at all. TestUploadFileLostAnswerIsUnknown drops the connection mid-upload and asserts an OutcomeUnknownError and exactly one attempt, so a lost answer is never retried. TestUploadUsesFileParamFromCanvas sets file_param to attachment[uploaded_data] and asserts the parts on the wire are the policy field then that name, with the filename intact. TestUploadLargeFileStreams sends 50 MB and asserts the request declared an exact Content-Length equal to the body it sent, that the file part is exactly 50 MB, and that its SHA-256 matches the file on disk, with each 1 KiB block filled differently so truncation or re-ordering fails the hash.

internal/cli/upload_test.go, through runCLI against the fake: TestUploadThreeSteps asserts the three requests in order, every one carrying the same Authorization and X-Job-Label, step 1 sent as application/x-www-form-urlencoded with name, size, content_type and on_duplicate=rename, step 3 keeping the uuid from the redirect, and the printed envelope's file and embed_src. TestUploadRefusesUploadURLOffGateway and TestUploadLostAnswerIsUnknown are the command's exit codes for the two client refusals above, 9 and 8. TestUploadOutsideWorkspaceRefused covers a path in another folder and a link inside the course folder pointing out, both exit 9 with nothing sent. TestUploadNormalModeNeedsCourse asserts --course is required outside Canvas Builder, exit 2.

CodeRabbit reviewed the patch and raised one finding, minor and valid: the copied http.Client kept its whole-exchange Timeout, which in Canvas Builder is approval_timeout + 30s, so a file big enough to outrun it would be cut off mid-stream and reported as an outcome nobody knows — the most expensive answer this command has, for a file that was probably landing fine. Its suggested fix was Timeout = 0, which was not taken: this command uses cmd.Context(), which carries no deadline, so a zero timeout means a hung gateway hangs the agent with no answer at all. The finding's own alternative was taken instead — uploadTimeout scales the bound with the file's size, at a megabyte a second, which on a machine whose Canvas is local is a rate only a stalled transfer falls below. TestUploadTimeoutScalesWithSize covers an empty file, 500 MB, and a caller that asked for no bound.
